big_idea: Game theory -- the formal study of strategic interaction between rational actors -- is not just an academic tool but a practical lens for everyday competitive and cooperative decisions, from business negotiation to poker to parenting, and this book by two leading economists translates its core results into plain language.

tool.label: Nash Equilibrium and Dominant Strategy Analysis
tool.text: The book teaches readers to map a strategic situation as a game -- the players, their moves, and their payoffs -- and then find a Nash equilibrium: a set of choices where no player can improve their outcome by unilaterally switching. A dominant strategy is a stronger case: a move that's best no matter what opponents do. The authors use the prisoner's dilemma to show how individually dominant strategies can produce a collectively worse outcome, and pair this with commitment strategy -- deliberately limiting your own future options to make a threat or promise credible.
tool.note: Reviewers note the 'art' framing oversells how directly game theory applies to messy real-world negotiations -- clean game-theoretic models require well-defined players, moves, and payoffs that rarely exist that cleanly in practice.

ideas.title: Sequential vs. simultaneous games
ideas.text: The book distinguishes games where players move in turn, where backward induction and foresight matter, from games where everyone moves at once.

ideas.title: Mixed strategies
ideas.text: When no pure choice is optimal, the book explains randomizing choices according to specific probabilities to avoid being predictably exploited.

ideas.title: Credible commitment and threats
ideas.text: A threat or promise only changes behavior if the other side believes you'll follow through -- the book catalogs real tactics for making commitments credible.

ideas.title: The focal point
ideas.text: In games with multiple possible equilibria, players often coordinate on a salient, obvious option even without communication.

ideas.title: Auction design and bidding traps
ideas.text: The book walks through the winner's curse -- why winning an auction for an uncertain-value item is itself evidence you overpaid.

ideas.title: Brinkmanship and escalation
ideas.text: Gradually escalating risk, rather than an all-or-nothing threat, can be used to extract concessions while limiting downside.

try_it: Before your next negotiation, write out the other side's likely payoffs for each of their possible moves, not just your own.
Identify one recurring price-war dynamic on your team or with a competitor and check whether it matches the prisoner's dilemma payoff structure.
Practice making one commitment this week specifically to make a promise credible to a counterpart.
Before entering a bid or auction situation, calculate what your win would tell you about whether you overvalued the item.
best_for: Readers with genuine intellectual curiosity about the underlying math/logic of strategic decision-making.
Negotiators and dealmakers who want a rigorous framework for anticipating counterparties' incentives.
less_useful: Readers wanting quick, tactical business advice -- this is closer to an accessible economics textbook than a management how-to guide.
Anyone allergic to math notation or formal logic puzzles.

related.why: Your Next Five Moves shares a chess-like, several-moves-ahead approach to business competition.
Good Strategy/Bad Strategy offers a complementary, less mathematical view of competitive positioning.
